description: Small team building an open-source web tool for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge: enter sky coordinates and watch SPHEREx images of that patch change over time.
summary:
NASA's SPHEREx telescope revisits the whole sky about every six months, and its first full data release (DR1) came out this month. Volunteers on Backyard Worlds have found more than 3,000 brown dwarf candidates by blinking WISE images, and we found no public tool that does this for SPHEREx images.

Wandering Pixels is a public website that plays SPHEREx images of any patch of sky as a movie across the telescope's visits. Pick a spot on a 3D Earth, look up at the sky from there, open a patch (or type a name or coordinates), then blink two images, subtract one from the other, click a spot to read its brightness at every wavelength, and overlay Gaia and WISE stars. We also measured how SPHEREx exposures at different wavelengths can and cannot be compared: a plain pair misreads a constant star more as the wavelength gap grows, and comparing each star's own fitted spectrum removes that. The tool shows how a search for a distant moving body works. It does not claim that any planet has been, or can be, found with it.
details:
What a visitor can do

  • Turn a 3D Earth, pick a place or click anywhere, then "Look up from here" to see the whole sky from horizon to zenith, with the year-one SPHEREx all-sky map behind it. That map does not show change.
  • Open a patch by pointing, typing a name or coordinates, or choosing a prepared target: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855-0714, RW Aurigae, R Draconis. Other positions are read live from NASA's archive.
  • Play the images across visits, blink two, or subtract one from the other (for the eye, no significance). Click a spot for its spectrum, overlay Gaia and WISE stars, and copy a link to the view.
  • Click a star for "Has it changed between visits?": a verdict with a reliability flag. Within about 3 arcminutes of any star brighter than magnitude 9 it is marked unreliable, so most neighbours of the five challenge targets are marked not reliable. A sixth prepared field, "Example: a star that varies", shows the readout on a real change: the eclipsing binary V391 Ophiuchi differs between visits by about 15 percent on the default detector, while a steady neighbour of the same brightness is consistent. The size of that change depends on which exposures happened to fall in eclipse. The browser code reproduces the reference analysis.
  • Try "Distant bodies": blink two visits a year apart, where stars cancel and a distant body would show as a bright and dark pair, then follow a body at an assumed distance on the visit six months away (live targets). "Try it with a simulated body" plants one.

What we measured

Two fields, public SPHEREx data. Detail: https://github.com/saamirkhrl/wandering-pixels/blob/main/docs/method.md

  • A plain pair misreads a constant star more as the wavelength gap grows (width 1.4 at a gap under half a channel, 8.7 over 10). Comparing each star's own fitted spectrum keeps it near 1.4 (slope +0.64 +/- 0.09 plain, +0.001 +/- 0.001 matched; 70 and 49 stars).
  • Visits six or twelve months apart do not line up in wavelength better than visits a week apart (typical gap about 5 channels), though 52 to 75 percent of exposures have a partner within one channel.
  • Archive coordinates register exposures to 0.04 to 0.06 pixel (0.22 to 0.39 arcsec), on 171 and 257 stars. Archive error bars are 1.2 to 1.4 times too small.
  • Epsilon Indi B's motion between visits matches Gaia DR3 to within 0.10 arcsec (its absolute position sits a constant (+0.2, -0.55) arcsec off, as expected for an unresolved pair). Saturated Barnard's Star still gives 1.68 pixels a year from its outer glow against 1.69 predicted.
  • Gaia DR3 4472819623984651392 (V391 Oph, G 12.7), classified as an eclipsing binary in Gaia DR3 (Rimoldini et al. 2023) that changes within a visit, stands out (root-mean-square z 18.2 against 0.9); one of two variables tested.
  • Fake moving stars in real Barnard's Star images were found half the time at AB 18.3 to 19.1 for 2 to 4 pixels of motion, and about AB 16 at 1 pixel. One field, flat spectrum, 30 trials per point: a small test.
  • The change statistic reaches |z| of 3 on about 0.9 percent of matched comparisons of steady stars. The 1 percent false-alarm rate holds for unblended, unsaturated stars of Gaia G 12 to 16.5, more than 3 arcminutes from any star brighter than G 9. Near saturated stars, or for blends, it can be tens of percent, and the site marks those results as not reliable.
  • Negative results: per-pixel matched images failed; three resampling kernels did not remove dipoles around bright stars.

The distant-body demonstration

We planted simulated 500 au bodies (AB 12.75 and 14.25) in real Barnard's Star exposures. Step one found the bright one as a pair 21.8 pixels apart (21.0 true). Step two read its distance as 505 au against 500; without the body's own motion, 462 au. With the distance known, the tracked stack reaches about AB 19.5; a blind search in this crowded field picks out the fake only down to about AB 14, because real stars leave residuals. This is a demonstration of a method, not a search. Single images reach about AB 18.5 to 19 (pre-launch figures); published Planet Nine models sit at 19 to 27 and an earlier WISE search reached 19.4. Single images cannot reach past earlier searches. Stacking every frame in the body's own frame could in principle go about one magnitude deeper than the WISE search at 3 to 4 microns. That would test only the warmest models, and it is not done here. No discovery is expected and the tool does not claim any planet.

Limits

  • Two fields; stars of Gaia G 12 to 16.5. Brighter stars, including Barnard's Star, RW Aurigae and R Draconis, are saturated; the site shows their images only.
  • WISE 0855-0714 is not seen: our 3 sigma limit near 4.6 microns, 16.8 AB, cannot constrain it (expected about 17.4 AB).
  • Matching works per star, not per pixel; difference images are not validated at pixel level.
  • Single runs on 2026-11-14 during an IRSA outage window: a prepared target's opening view downloaded 119 to 170 KB in 1.3 to 2.0 s. Of 20 live archive searches, 15 answered (median 10.9 s, most partial) and 5 failed after about 20 s; a live initial look took 3.9 to 13.8 s and 5.5 to 6.0 MB.

Prior art

WiseView (https://byw.tools/wiseview) does blink, difference, shift-and-add and a Gaia overlay for WISE, and the challenge points to it as a similar tool. SPXQuery and SPIFF (Gagne et al. 2026) work with SPHEREx photometry and spectra, as far as we could tell, and IRSA's Data Explorer documents no blink or difference mode. Our search was time-limited. We add a SPHEREx image viewer with blink, difference and distance following in the browser, and the wavelength-mismatch validation.

How the project addresses the challenge

The challenge asks for a public web tool that shows SPHEREx images of the sky and makes it easy to see how they change over time. The site does this for any position, with the five named targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855-0714, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) ready to open. It also covers the optional items in the challenge text: spectra on the fly, adding and subtracting images from different times, Gaia and WISE overlays, coordinates in the link, and contamination flags. The measurements above say how far a visitor can trust a comparison between exposures taken at different wavelengths.

How it was developed

TypeScript, Vite, three.js for the globe and sky, and astronomy-engine for sun, rise and set times. The browser reads SPHEREx Level 2 FITS files straight from NASA's public S3 bucket with HTTP range requests and does the alignment and image maths itself. Small relay functions (Vercel functions) handle archive search, Gaia, WISE and name lookup. Five challenge targets are prepared as cached files. Validation is Python (astropy, astroquery, photutils, reproject, scipy, numpy, matplotlib, aiohttp, fsspec, s3fs, requests) run with uv. Hosting is on Vercel. Code and licences are listed in the README of the repository.

Links

Live site: https://wandering-pixels.vercel.app

Source code (Apache License 2.0): https://github.com/saamirkhrl/wandering-pixels

Demo video (26.5 seconds; the narration voice is AI generated, the picture is a real screen capture of the live site): https://wandering-pixels.vercel.app/demo.mp4

Use of AI tools

AI coding assistants were used to write code, run analyses, draft text and generate the demo narration audio. This was done under the team's direction and review. The code, analyses and written material of this project were produced with that assistance.
